source: Daw, Niv, Dayan (2005) Uncertainty-based competition between prefrontal and dorsolateral striatal systems for behavioral control
finding: Two controllers: a prefrontal tree-search (model-based) system and a dorsolateral striatal caching (temporal-difference, model-free) system. Each keeps a Bayesian posterior over action values. The agent trusts the controller with the lower posterior variance (uncertainty) for each action.
numbers: Simulated absorbing MDP tasks; Fig 5 means over 250 runs, Fig 6 means over 1000 runs; s.e.m. negligible.
limits: Theory paper with simulations only; no new human or rat data. Arbitration by uncertainty does not price the time or effort cost of planning explicitly.
agent_relevance: Gives the first formal arbiter: pick the source whose estimate is least uncertain. A cheap proxy for an S0 gate if an uncertainty estimate for 'direct answer' vs 'reasoned answer' exists.

source: Daw, Niv, Dayan (2005) - why each system is uncertain
finding: Tree search is more data-efficient: one observation updates values at all states at once. Caching is slow because bootstrapping delays propagation. So the tree is more certain early in training in all simulations. Tree search also adds 'computational noise' that grows with each search step (pruning, partial paths); cached values have almost none.
numbers: Both systems start with matched prior uncertainty; the tree is more confident early. Late: for the action nearest reward (magazine entry) the tree stays more certain; for the action far from reward (lever press, one extra search iteration) the cache wins asymptotically.
quote: This is because under prefrontal tree search, any particular morsel of experience immediately propagates to influence the estimates of action values at all states
limits: The computational-noise term is an assumption, not measured. Depends on the assumed rate of task change that sets the effective data horizon.
agent_relevance: Search noise accumulates with depth: deeper reasoning chains add error. This is the formal reason to cap planning depth and prefer a cached/known answer on well-practised problem classes.

source: Daw, Niv, Dayan (2005) - devaluation results explained
finding: The model reproduces the animal devaluation literature: moderately trained lever pressing is sensitive to outcome devaluation (tree controls); extensively trained lever pressing is insensitive (cache controls); the action nearest reward (magazine entry) stays devaluation-sensitive even after heavy training; with two actions for two outcomes the tree stays in control after extensive training.
numbers: Single action task: cache takes over for the distal action with training. Two-action/two-outcome task (Fig 6): experience is split across more states, so the cache is less data-efficient and tree control persists.
limits: Qualitative match to published rat data; no direct fit with parameters. Authors note the dorsomedial striatum may belong to the tree system, not the cache.
agent_relevance: Planning should hand over to a cache only when the same problem class recurs often and is stable; variety keeps planning alive. A design rule for when S0 may route to 'direct'.

source: Daw, Niv, Dayan (2005) - predictions and open questions
finding: Predicts that reversals or unexpected task change restore tree control, that lesions disabling either system shift control, and that over-training plus task simplicity favours the cache while action-reward proximity and frequent reversals favour search. Notes monkey caudate/PFC reversal recordings could not yet discriminate the two readings.
numbers: No numbers; discussion section.
limits: Neural substrate of the uncertainty signal is said to have limited evidence (population codes, cholinergic and noradrenergic ideas are only suggestions).
agent_relevance: Change in the task is the trigger to re-plan. Maps to G1: doubt only on a signal (a failed check or surprise), not on a schedule.

source: Daw, Gershman, Seymour, Dayan, Dolan (2011) Model-based influences on humans' choices and striatal prediction errors - design
finding: The two-step task. Stage 1 choice between two options leads to one of two stage-2 states with fixed transition probabilities 0.7 common and 0.3 rare. Stage 2 pays with probabilities that drift as Gaussian random walks. Model-free predicts repeat after reward regardless of transition; model-based predicts repeat after reward only if the transition was common.
numbers: N = 17 healthy adults (5 female), mean age 25.8. 201 trials per person in three blocks of 67, 50 practice trials, 1.5T fMRI. Reward walk SD 0.025 with reflecting bounds 0.25 and 0.75. Paid 20% of displayed amount.
limits: Small fMRI sample. Subjects were told transitions are fixed and reward probabilities drift. Later work (Kool 2016, Akam 2015) shows the task design weakens the payoff for planning.
agent_relevance: The standard paradigm that nearly every later study (and any LLM test of planning versus habit) copies. Gives a clean behavioural signature to look for in an agent's choices.

source: Daw et al. (2011) - behaviour
finding: Choices showed both signatures at once. Reward main effect and reward-by-transition interaction were both significant, so people mix model-free and model-based control. The transition main effect was not significant.
numbers: Logistic regression, hierarchical: reward p < 1e-8; reward x transition p < 5e-5; transition p = .5; constant (perseveration) p < 5e-12. Reward effect positive for 14 of 17 subjects; interaction positive for 10 of 17.
limits: Effect sizes are not given as stay probabilities in the text (only a figure). Individual interaction estimates were noisy: only 7 of 17 showed both a positive reward effect and a positive interaction.
agent_relevance: The mixture, not a pure mode, is the human default. A scaffold should expect blended behaviour and gate by degree, not by switch.

source: Daw et al. (2011) - hybrid model and model comparison
finding: A hybrid reinforcement-learning model fits better than pure model-free or pure model-based. Value of the first-stage action is a weighted mix: w times model-based value plus (1-w) times model-free (TD lambda) value. Median w = 0.39 so people are about 61% model-free in this task.
numbers: Table 2: hybrid -LL 3364; TD-only 3418 (log Bayes factor 30.0); model-based-only 3501 (82.4); lambda=0 3452 (62.9); lambda=1 3392 (8.87). Exceedance probability hybrid .92. Median w 0.39 (IQR .29 to .59), differs from 0 and 1 (sign test P < .005); median lambda 0.57; median alpha1 0.54; median beta1 5.19; perseveration p 0.11. Mixed-effects fit used for fMRI: w mean 0.51, SD 0.31.
limits: Model comparison on the same 17 people. w depends on parameter trade-offs and on task design; later work shows w moves with task payoff (Kool 2016: median 0.27 vs 0.48).
agent_relevance: The w weight is the single number to track for a planned-versus-cached mix. An S0 gate could output a w-like mixing weight between direct and reasoned answer.

source: Daw et al. (2011) - striatal prediction errors
finding: Ventral striatal prediction error (BOLD) reflects both model-free and model-based information, not just model-free. The neural correlate of the model-based difference regressor overlapped the model-free signal, and its strength tracked each person's behavioural w. This argues against a clean split where striatum is only model-free.
numbers: Ventral striatum RPE: left (-12,10,4) and right (10,12,-4), p < .001 cluster-corrected. Conjunction right (12,16,-6) p < .01 whole-brain corrected. Correlation with behavioural w in right ventral striatum peak (14,20,-6), small-volume p < .01; ROI r^2 = .28, p = .027. Start-of-trial interaction vs w: r^2 = .32, p = .017. vmPFC conjunction only at relaxed threshold p < .005 uncorrected.
limits: fMRI N = 17, correlations from one ROI, small-volume corrections. Authors read it as integration of the two systems' values.
agent_relevance: Values from planning and from habit appear combined into one signal, not kept apart. An agent should merge both estimates into one decision value rather than hand off completely.

source: Glascher, Daw, Dayan, O'Doherty (2010) States versus rewards: dissociable neural prediction error signals underlying model-based and model-free reinforcement learning
finding: A separate learning signal for model-based control: a state prediction error (SPE, surprise about which state followed) found in posterior intraparietal sulcus and lateral prefrontal cortex, distinct from the reward prediction error in ventral striatum. SPE appeared even in session 1 when no rewards were given.
numbers: N = 18 analysed (20 recruited, 2 excluded). Two sessions of 80 trials; transitions 0.7/0.3; outcomes 0c, 10c or 25c. Hybrid AIC 2414.56 vs SARSA 2439.88 vs FORWARD 2643.49; hybrid vs SARSA chi2(2) = 21.32, p = 2.35e-5. SPE: left lateral PFC (-45,9,33) Z = 5.62 p < .001; left IPS (-27,-54,45) Z = 5.29 p = .004; RPE left ventral striatum (-12,6,-9) Z = 5.18 p = .006. Right pIPS SPE vs early choice accuracy r = 0.57, p = .013. Mean RPE-SPE correlation -0.37.
limits: Single parameter set for all subjects. Authors note SPE could partly be general attention or salience, though it beat unsigned RPE. Left and right PFC SPE did not correlate with behaviour (r = .28, .38).
agent_relevance: Model-based learning is driven by prediction error on structure, model-free by prediction error on reward. An analogue for an agent: update its world model from surprising outputs (code-checked failures) and its habits from outcome.

source: Keramati, Dezfouli, Piray (2011) Speed/accuracy trade-off between the habitual and the goal-directed processes
finding: The key theory for an S0 gate. Arbitrate by value of information: the goal-directed (model-based) system is run for an action only if the value of perfect information (VPI) about that action, computed from the habitual system's own uncertainty, exceeds the cost of deliberating. Cost = deliberation time times the average reward rate (opportunity cost of time). If not, use the cached mean.
numbers: Habitual system = Kalman-style TD with a distribution over each Q value. VPI has a closed form (Dearden et al.). Average reward is an exponentially weighted moving average. Simulated outcome devaluation: moderate training (40 trials) gives about a 50% fall in responding for the alternative action after devaluation; extensive training (240 trials): deliberation time falls to zero after about 100 trials and devaluation has no effect. Means over 3000 runs.
quote: If VPI exceeds the cost, the goal-directed system
limits: Only simulations. Exact parameter values and Methods were not in the text read. Model predicts a linear rise of deliberation with number of choices early on, but data follow Hick's law (logarithmic). Predicts that sensitivity persists with similar-valued concurrent options; authors say this was untested.
agent_relevance: Near-exact blueprint: plan only if the expected gain from the extra reasoning (VPI) is larger than its cost (tokens or time times value of time). Implementable in S0 with a cheap uncertainty estimate and a token budget.

source: Keramati et al. (2011) - behavioural predictions
finding: Four simulated datasets: (1) devaluation after moderate vs extensive training; (2) concurrent schedule where two levers of equal value stay goal-directed after 240 trials; (3) reversal learning where reaction time is higher while searching and rises again after reversal; (4) choice reaction time versus number of choices.
numbers: Concurrent schedule: after 240 trials VPI stays above cost so devaluation sensitivity remains. Reversal: reaction time higher in search than apply period; movement time unaffected by learning. Choice RT: after training deliberation does not depend on number of choices.
limits: A fixed non-deliberation time had to be added to match reaction times. Linear versus logarithmic mismatch with Hick's law. No fit to individual data.
agent_relevance: Predicts that planning cost rises again after a reversal or change: when a check fails, planning should switch back on. Matches the signal-triggered design in G1.

source: Keramati et al. (2011) - neural mapping and rival accounts
finding: Phasic dopamine carries the prediction error that trains habits. Tonic dopamine carries the average reward rate, which sets the cost of deliberating. The paper contrasts itself with Daw et al. 2005 (uncertainty-only arbitration), Shah and Barto, Niv et al. (vigor) and Dickinson's contingency account.
numbers: No numbers; discussion.
limits: The tonic dopamine claim is a hypothesis. Daw 2005 predicts a switch to caching with two same-outcome choices; Keramati predicts they stay goal-directed, a testable difference.
agent_relevance: Two competing arbitration rules exist: uncertainty (Daw 2005) and cost-of-time against information value (Keramati 2011). The second matches our token-budget gate.

source: Akam, Costa, Dayan (2015) Simple plans or sophisticated habits? State, transition and learning interactions in the two-step task
finding: Model-free agents can look model-based in the two-step task. Simple changes to the task structure create correlations between action values at the start of a trial and later events, so stay-probability analysis can mislead. A 'reward-as-cue' model-free agent that uses where the last reward was found as a state cue mimics the model-based interaction, even under more refined analyses.
numbers: Simulations: Q(1), Q(0), model-based, reward-as-cue (4 states) and latent-state (Bayesian 2-state) agents; 30% rare transitions; errors are SEM across sessions. No human sample.
limits: Simulation paper, but widely cited as a warning. A suggested correction for the start-of-trial correlation works. The task also needs stochasticity to discriminate strategies but determinism to make planning worthwhile.
agent_relevance: A reasoning-looking pattern can come from a learned shortcut. For LLMs: a correct-looking plan can be a memorised mapping, so test with variants where the shortcut breaks (G3).

source: Akam et al. (2015) - the stochasticity versus payoff trade-off
finding: The task faces a design conflict: transitions need to be random so strategies can be told apart, yet determinism is needed so effort in planning pays off. Strategies that automatise by finding the few relevant states ('sophisticated habits') are plausible in repeated planning problems and are of interest in themselves.
numbers: No single number; qualitative argument backed by the agent simulations.
limits: Companion to Kool 2016: both show that the standard w estimate can be a poor measure of planning.
agent_relevance: Repeated problem classes lead to habits that look like planning. A reason for S0 to measure whether a class really needs search, using held-out variants.

source: Kool, Cushman, Gershman (2016) When does model-based control pay off?
finding: The original two-step task gives almost no reward advantage for being model-based, so there is no real accuracy-versus-effort trade-off to arbitrate. Five factors cause this: low distinguishability of options, slow drift, rare transitions, a second-stage choice that dilutes first-stage importance, and weak binary outcomes. A redesigned task fixes them and people then increase model-based control.
numbers: Reward probabilities 0.25 to 0.75 give a mean difference ~1/6; drift SD 0.025. Combining all five factors raised the trade-off strength ~230 times; 6.9 SD above four-factor tasks. Human sample: 406 on Mechanical Turk (199 novel, 207 Daw task), 381 model-fit. Median w 0.27 (Daw) vs 0.48 (novel), z = 3.31, p < .001. Correlation of w with adjusted reward rate r = 0.55 (novel) vs 0.10 (Daw, p = .15); group difference t(377) = 4.71. Corrected reward gain 0.01 vs 0.51.
quote: describe a version of the task that formally and empirically obtains an accuracy-demand trade-off
limits: Online sample; w is fit on a different task design so cross-task comparison is indirect. A summary-tool read flagged that some percentage statements in the paper do not match the listed values; use the raw numbers.
agent_relevance: Trade-off strength: how much model-based control gains reward over model-free. Authors describe a version of the task that obtains this trade-off.

source: Kool, Cushman, Gershman (2016) - how it bears on arbitration
finding: Failures to find model-based control in earlier work may reflect tasks where planning does not pay. This is strong empirical support for cost-benefit arbitration: when planning pays, people plan more; when it does not, they do not.
numbers: Daw task predicted reward 0.52 at w=0 rising by only 0.002 at w=1. Novel task 0.58 at w=0 rising to 1.25 at w=1.
limits: Demonstrates behaviour change, not the exact decision rule.
agent_relevance: For an LLM benchmark of planning, check that planning actually pays in the test; otherwise a null result is uninformative.

source: Kool, Gershman, Cushman (2017) Cost-benefit arbitration between multiple reinforcement-learning systems
finding: Two experiments: people raise model-based control when it yields greater accuracy than model-free control, especially when rewards for accuracy are amplified; when the two systems reach equal accuracy they do not respond to the amplification. Read from search-result abstract only.
numbers: Exact N and effect sizes not obtained this session.
limits: Not opened; numbers missing. Check full text before citing numbers. A 2025 failed extension to social learning exists (title seen in OpenAlex: No Evidence for Cost-Benefit Arbitration Between Social Learning Strategies), not read.
agent_relevance: Direct human evidence for the cost-benefit rule in S0: spend effort in proportion to what correct answers are worth.

source: Otto, Gershman, Markman, Daw (2013) The curse of planning: taxing the central executive
finding: A concurrent numerical Stroop working-memory load reduced the model-based signature in the two-step task: people leaned on model-free control under load, and used both when unloaded. A second experiment conceptually replicated it. Reported from abstract and secondary snippets only.
numbers: Design as described by a search snippet: 300 two-step trials, with a numerical Stroop task on 150 selected load trials. Exact N and statistics not obtained.
limits: Not opened (PMC page blocked). Cite numbers only after checking the full text.
agent_relevance: Planning competes for limited working resources; for an LLM the analogue is context and token budget. Under budget pressure expect reduced planning.

source: Keramati, Smittenaar, Dolan, Dayan (2016) Adaptive integration of habits into depth-limited planning defines a habitual-goal-directed spectrum
finding: People plan until they hit a state whose cached value they can trust, then use that value instead of searching to the end. Under time pressure they stop planning sooner. Depth k = 0 (pure habit), 1 (plan until habit), 2 (full plan). Evidence for a speed-accuracy trade-off controlling planning depth, with habit values folded into planning.
numbers: Three-step task, 70/30 transitions. High-resource group (n = 15) had 2 s to respond; low-resource group (n = 15) had 700 ms. High-resource: pure planning effect after rewarded (P < 0.001) and unrewarded trials (P < 0.001); plan-until-habit effect only after unrewarded trials (P < 0.002), not rewarded (P = 0.073). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
limits: Between-subject, 15 per group, a single task. The full group contrast was not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Planning depth is the dial, not on/off. A scaffold can bound depth and bootstrap from a cached estimate at the horizon.

source: Gillan, Kosinski, Whelan, Phelps, Daw (2016) Characterizing a psychiatric symptom dimension related to deficits in goal-directed control
finding: Large online study showing individual differences in model-based control (the two-step task) map onto a compulsivity and intrusive-thought symptom dimension rather than onto diagnostic categories. Deficits were specific to that factor.
numbers: N = 548 in the first sample, plus an independent replication sample. Other factors null: Factor 1 beta -0.001 (p = .92), Factor 3 beta 0.013 (p = .24); depression beta -0.01, p = .385; trait anxiety p = .498; schizotypy beta -0.017, p = .14. A factor onto which addiction and impulsivity load negatively predicted more goal-directed control (beta 0.031, p = .014). No evidence of nonlinearity.
limits: Online self-report; effect sizes small (betas about 0.03). The model-based measure inherits the task limits found by Kool 2016.
agent_relevance: Shows the model-based weight w is a stable individual trait with real-world meaning, so it is a reliable thing to measure across a population of agents.

source: Otto, Skatova, Madlon-Kay, Daw (2015) Model-based learning protects against forming habits
finding: People who showed more model-based learning in the two-step task later were more sensitive to outcome devaluation, so model-based learning protects against forming habits. A conceptual replication in a new sample confirmed it. This ties the lab two-step measure to the classic devaluation test of habit.
numbers: Experiment 1: 90 online participants. Reward x transition x devaluation interaction p = .003 (reward p < .001, reward x transition p = .020); one SD below mean devaluation sensitivity removes model-based learning altogether. Experiment 2: 95 new participants; habit group showed reduced model-based signature, p < .001; consumption related to devaluation sensitivity (p = .05) but did not explain the link (p = .006).
limits: Online samples. Correlational; relies on devaluation sensitivity as the habit measure. The 0.6 split of devaluation sensitivity is arbitrary.
agent_relevance: Links the two paradigms: the model-based weight predicts whether behaviour stays flexible to a change in goal value. For agents: test habits by changing the goal and checking whether the output changes.

source: Dayan and Berridge (2014) Model-based and model-free Pavlovian reward learning: revaluation, revision and revelation
finding: Pavlovian (stimulus-outcome) prediction can also be model-based: states of the body and brain can change cue values at once, with no new learning. This extends the model-free versus model-based distinction beyond instrumental choice and shows the cached versus computed split is general.
numbers: Review; no new data.
limits: A theoretical review; cited evidence not individually checked here.
agent_relevance: Even a prediction (not only an action) can be cached or recomputed; the S0 gate should apply to answers and to evaluations.

source: Dickinson (1985) Actions and habits: the development of behavioural autonomy
finding: Founding behavioural distinction: goal-directed actions depend on knowledge of the action-outcome contingency and the current value of the outcome; habits are stimulus-response links not sensitive to outcome value. Extensive training and ratio versus interval schedules shift behaviour toward habit.
numbers: Numbers not collected; from background, not opened.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Source of the devaluation test used as the behavioural gold standard of planning.

source: Adams and Dickinson (1981) Instrumental responding following reinforcer devaluation
finding: Rats trained to press a lever for a food pellet, then given the pellet paired with illness, pressed less in extinction. This shows responding used a representation of the outcome. Later work showed extensive training removes this effect.
numbers: Numbers not collected; not opened.
limits: Not opened this session; later work shows the effect depends on training amount and schedule (see Daw 2005 simulations).
agent_relevance: Original devaluation method; the test that separates model-based from model-free behaviour.

source: Sutton and Barto (1998) Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction; Sutton (1990) Dyna
finding: Formal basis: model-free methods (temporal-difference, Q-learning, SARSA) learn cached values from experience; model-based methods learn transition and reward models and plan with them. Dyna interleaves real experience with planning updates using a learned model.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers collected.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Dyna is the closest classic design for an agent that mixes direct experience with replayed planning, like using remembered solved cases plus fresh reasoning.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating cognitive maps and planning in large language models with CogEval
finding: Eight LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, text-davinci-003, Bard, Cohere-xlarge, Claude-1, LLaMA-13B, Alpaca-7B) were tested on planning tasks built from human experiments. They showed competence on simple structures but failed in systematic tests: invented edges that do not exist, took longer paths than the shortest, and got trapped in loops. No sign of out-of-the-box planning.
numbers: Shortest path to a state one cluster away: GPT-4 success 0 of 30 at temperature 0; at temperature 0.5 or 1, repeating 30 runs, success could not exceed 10%.
limits: Prompts based on human tasks, but 2023-era models; newer reasoning models may do better. Single prompt format per model.
agent_relevance: Without a search scaffold, LLMs do not plan reliably over relational structure. Argues for program-side search with code-checked steps rather than free reasoning.

source: Coda-Forno, Binz, Wang, Schulz (2024) CogBench: a large language model walks into a psychology lab
finding: Seven tasks, ten behavioural metrics. The Daw two-step task measures model-basedness. Models able to solve the two-step task show model-based behaviour at least on par with humans, with GPT-4 well above human level. Model-basedness rises with parameter count; training-set size and code data had no significant effect. Take-a-step-back prompting raised model-basedness; chain-of-thought mainly helped probabilistic reasoning.
numbers: Parameter-count effect on model-basedness beta = 0.481 +/- 0.22, z = 4.2, p < 0.001. Fig 5 compares chain-of-thought and step-back to baseline over five models with inverse-variance weighting; exact per-model values not extracted.
limits: Text two-step variant with a story prompt, 70% fixed transitions, default 100 simulations; the weak planning payoff found by Kool 2016 applies equally. Reading LLM w as planning is contested, since LLMs can mimic stay patterns through in-context cues (Akam 2015).
agent_relevance: First broad measurement of the model-based weight in LLMs; shows prompting can shift it, a handle for an S0 gate to move a model from habit to plan.

source: Demircan, Saanum, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) Sparse autoencoders reveal temporal difference learning in large language models
finding: Llama 3 70B solves simple in-context reinforcement-learning problems. Sparse autoencoder features in the residual stream match temporal-difference errors and Q-values, and interventions on them change behaviour. So an LLM can implement a model-free value-learning computation in-context.
numbers: Three tasks; causal interventions on SAE features change TD error and Q-values. Specific effect sizes not extracted.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read in this session; applies to simple RL tasks, not planning in text.
agent_relevance: Shows in-context caching of values is a real mechanism in LLMs; planning versus cache can be seen in activations, not only in outputs.
